---
title: "Encapsulation: what a class keeps to itself"
---

Every field you wrote in the last chapter was open to the whole file. Any line
in `index.ts` could reach into an object and put any value into any of its
fields, and TypeScript nodded along. That works for an hour. Then one line
writes a number the rest of the class was never built for.

## A score of minus five {#sec-encapsulation-nonsense}

1. Create a new app `encapsulation-experiment` from our template inside
   `coursework/`.
2. In `index.html`, replace everything between `<body>` and `</body>` with
   this:

   ```html
   <h1>Score</h1>
   <p id="scoreLine">Score: 0</p>
   <script src="./src/index.ts" type="module"></script>
   ```

3. Replace everything in `src/index.ts` with this:

   ```ts
   class Score {
     points: number = 0;

     add(amount: number) {
       this.points += amount;
     }
   }

   const scoreLine = document.querySelector<HTMLParagraphElement>('#scoreLine');

   if (!scoreLine) {
     throw new Error('The page has no score line');
   }

   const score = new Score();
   score.add(10);
   score.points = -5;

   scoreLine.textContent = `Score: ${score.points}`;
   ```

4. Run `npm start`.

The page says `Score: -5`, and nothing warned you. The class is written as if
`points` only ever grows, and the line `score.points = -5;` walks past all of
that. A public field is an open door: anyone may write anything the type
allows, and `-5` is a `number`.

## The private keyword {#sec-encapsulation-private}

Put `private` in front of the field:

```ts
private points: number = 0;
```

VS Code draws a red squiggle, and `npx tsc --noEmit` names both places:

```
src/index.ts(17,7): error TS2341: Property 'points' is private and only accessible within class 'Score'.
src/index.ts(19,41): error TS2341: Property 'points' is private and only accessible within class 'Score'.
```

Line 17 is the assignment you wanted to stop. Line 19 is the display line,
which only reads the value, and `private` shuts that one too. Private means
private for reading as well.

So give the class the ways in that the outside really needs. Delete
`score.points = -5;` and add two members to `Score`:

```ts
subtract(amount: number) {
  this.points -= amount;
  if (this.points < 0) {
    this.points = 0;
  }
}

current(): number {
  return this.points;
}
```

Now read the score through the method:

```ts
scoreLine.textContent = `Score: ${score.current()}`;
```

Call `score.subtract(30)` on a score of 10 and the page shows `Score: 0`. A
negative score has become impossible, because the only ways in are `add` and
`subtract`, and `subtract` knows the rule.

## The rule lives inside the class {#sec-encapsulation-invariant}

A sentence like "a score never goes below zero" is an **invariant**: something
a class promises about itself at every moment, whatever the rest of the program
does.

An invariant holds only if every line that changes the value respects it.
Making the field private cuts those lines down to the methods of one class, and
they all fit on one screen. **Encapsulation** is the name for that move: the
data sits packed inside the object, and the outside gets methods instead of
fields.

`private` is a rule TypeScript enforces while you write. The JavaScript that
reaches the browser has no lock on the field, and somebody poking at your page
in the developer console can still change it. It guards your program against
the code you write on a tired Friday afternoon.

## Fields that are set once and never again {#sec-encapsulation-readonly}

Some values belong to an object from the moment it is created and should never
move afterwards, such as the width of a board or the maximum a score can reach.
`readonly` says so:

```ts
class Score {
  private points: number = 0;
  readonly maxPoints: number;

  constructor(maxPoints: number) {
    this.maxPoints = maxPoints;
  }

  // add, subtract, and current as before
}
```

Create the object with `const score = new Score(100);`. Reading
`score.maxPoints` anywhere is fine, and it is meant to be, because the
scoreboard has to print the maximum somewhere. Writing it gets you
`error TS2540: Cannot assign to 'maxPoints' because it is a read-only
property.`

A `readonly` field can be given its value where it is declared or inside the
constructor. Every later assignment is an error, inside the class as much as
outside. `private` decides who may touch a field, `readonly` decides when, and
plenty of fields want both.

## Getters and setters {#sec-encapsulation-getters}

`score.current()` does its job, and it reads like an action, when all it does
is look up a number. TypeScript can keep the field private and still let the
outside read it like a field:

```ts
class Score {
  private pointsValue: number = 0;
  readonly maxPoints: number;

  // constructor as before

  get points(): number {
    return this.pointsValue;
  }
}
```

The stored value now has a name of its own, `pointsValue`, and it stays
private. `get points()` is a method the outside reads without parentheses, as
`score.points`. Assigning to it is still an error, so the door the class wanted
shut stays shut.

A getter earns its place when it computes instead of handing a field back. A
stopwatch keeps no field with the elapsed time: it keeps the clock reading from
when it started, and `get elapsed()` does the arithmetic when somebody asks.

The other direction exists too:

```ts
set points(value: number) {
  this.pointsValue = Math.min(Math.max(value, 0), this.maxPoints);
}
```

With that setter in the class, `score.points = 500;` compiles again, and on a
score whose `maxPoints` is 100 the value that gets stored is 100. The outside
writes what it likes and the class decides what to keep.

Setters stay rare in this course. `score.points = score.points - 30;` says
nothing about why the score dropped, while `score.subtract(30);` does. Reach
for a setter only when the outside really is just setting a value that the
class has to check.

## The short way to write a constructor field {#sec-encapsulation-parameter-properties}

`maxPoints` cost three lines: the field, the constructor parameter, and the
assignment between them. TypeScript folds all three into one:

```ts
class Score {
  private pointsValue: number = 0;

  constructor(private readonly maxPoints: number) {}

  get points(): number {
    return this.pointsValue;
  }
}
```

An access keyword in front of a constructor parameter turns that parameter into
a field of the same name and fills it before the constructor body runs. Drop
`readonly` and the field can still change from inside the class; write
`readonly` on its own and the field is readable from outside and locked
everywhere. The empty `{}` is a constructor body with nothing left to do, and
only constructor parameters work this way.

## protected, one chapter early {#sec-encapsulation-protected}

A third keyword sits next to `private` and `readonly`. `protected` closes a
member to the outside exactly like `private`, and opens it to classes that are
built on top of this one. Building one class on top of another is what the next
chapter is about, so `protected` has nothing to guard yet. It is here so the
word is not new when a `protected` field turns up in front of you.

## Changing the inside without breaking the outside {#sec-encapsulation-why}

Invariants are one reason to hide a field. The other shows up the day you
change your mind about how the class works.

Say the score has to remember how it got there, so the game can float a
"plus 10" over the board. The class stops keeping one number and keeps an array
of every change instead, and `get points()` adds that array up. Every line
outside still writes `score.add(10)` and reads `score.points`, and none of them
has to be touched.

That rewrite is painless only because nothing outside ever reached for
`pointsValue`. The public part of a class is a promise you have to keep, and
the private part is where you may still change your mind.

::: {.research title="Clock readings and tidy numbers"}
The two exercises below need four answers this chapter does not give. Without
them your stopwatch cannot measure anything, its display reads `1:7.3` instead
of `01:07.3`, and your account page proudly shows a balance of
`90.30000000000001`.

1. Both `Date.now()` and `performance.now()` hand you a number of
   milliseconds. What does each of them count from, and which one is the better
   choice for measuring how long something took?
2. Your stopwatch has to show `07` seconds, not `7`. Which string method pads a
   short string out to a fixed length, and what do its two arguments mean?
3. A balance of `90.3` has to appear as `90.30`. Which method of a number does
   that, and what kind of value does it give back?
4. A getter is read without parentheses. Write `watch.elapsed()` with
   parentheses anyway and let TypeScript answer. What does the error say, and
   what does it suggest?

Padding a number and fixing its decimal places come back in almost every exam
task that prints a value, so those two have to work without looking them up.
:::

## Exercise: a stopwatch {#sec-encapsulation-stopwatch}

A `Stopwatch` class with three private numbers inside it, and a page that shows
the time as `mm:ss.t` and never touches those numbers.

1. Create a new app from our template inside `coursework/`.
2. In `index.html`, replace everything between `<body>` and `</body>` with
   this:

   ```html
   <h1>Stopwatch</h1>

   <p id="display">00:00.0</p>

   <p>
     <button id="startButton" type="button">Start</button>
     <button id="stopButton" type="button">Stop</button>
     <button id="resetButton" type="button">Reset</button>
   </p>

   <script src="./src/index.ts" type="module"></script>
   ```

3. Create `src/styles.css` and give `#display` a monospace font family at about
   `3rem`, so the digits keep their places while they run. Replace everything
   in `src/index.ts` with `import './styles.css';`, then run `npm start`: big
   digits and three buttons that do nothing yet.
4. Write `class Stopwatch` in `src/index.ts`, under the import line. Give it
   three private fields with explicit types: `startTime`
   (a clock reading, starts at 0), `accumulated` (the milliseconds collected by
   earlier runs, starts at 0), and `running` (a boolean, starts as `false`).
5. Add `start()`. When the watch is already running it returns immediately.
   Otherwise it stores the current clock reading in `startTime` and sets
   `running` to `true`. Research question 1 tells you which function gives you
   that reading.
6. Add `stop()`. When the watch is not running it returns immediately.
   Otherwise it adds the time that has passed since `startTime` to
   `accumulated` and sets `running` to `false`.
7. Add `reset()`, which sets `accumulated` back to 0 and `running` to `false`.
8. Add `get elapsed(): number`. While the watch runs, the answer is
   `accumulated` plus the time since `startTime`. While it stands still, the
   answer is `accumulated` on its own.
9. Below the class, select the display and the three buttons with
   `document.querySelector<T>` and throw an error when any of them is missing.
   Then create the watch with `const watch = new Stopwatch();`.
10. Write a helper `const format = (milliseconds: number): string => { ... };`
    that returns text in the shape `mm:ss.t`: whole minutes, then seconds from
    0 to 59, then one digit for tenths of a second. Minutes and seconds are
    always two characters wide, which is research question 2.
11. Show the time with an animation loop, the same shape as the ball in the
    animation chapter:

    ```ts
    const tick = () => {
      display.textContent = format(watch.elapsed);
      requestAnimationFrame(tick);
    };

    requestAnimationFrame(tick);
    ```

12. Give each button a `click` listener that calls `start`, `stop`, or `reset`.
    Click Start and the digits run. Stop freezes them, Start picks up where it
    stopped, and Reset puts `00:00.0` back on the page.
13. Try to cheat: add `watch.accumulated = 60000;` at the end of the file and
    run `npx tsc --noEmit`. The compiler refuses, which is the point of the
    whole exercise. Delete the line again.

### Optional: buttons that know the state {#sec-encapsulation-stopwatch-toggle}

Give `Stopwatch` a getter `get isRunning(): boolean`, then set
`startButton.disabled = watch.isRunning;` and
`stopButton.disabled = !watch.isRunning;` inside the animation loop. The
buttons gray themselves out, and the page reads the flag without ever being
able to change it.

## Exercise: an account that refuses to go negative {#sec-encapsulation-bank}

The page you copy in already runs, and it lets you take out more money than the
account holds.

{{< exercise bank-account >}}

1. Run `npm start`. The page shows a balance of 100, a number field, and two
   buttons. Deposit 10 twice and the balance climbs to 120.
2. Now type 500 and click Withdraw. The balance drops to `-380` and the page
   prints it without a murmur. Open `src/index.ts`: the account is the object
   literal `const account = { balance: 100 };`, and both listeners do
   arithmetic on `account.balance` directly. The rule that a balance never goes
   below zero lives only in your head.
3. Write `class BankAccount` at the top of the file, above the object literal.
   Give it one private field, `balanceValue: number`.
4. Give the class a constructor with two parameters: `readonly owner: string`
   as a parameter property, and a plain `startBalance: number` that the
   constructor body assigns to `balanceValue`.
5. Add `get balance(): number`, which hands back `balanceValue`.
6. Add `deposit(amount: number): boolean`. When `amount` is not a number
   (`Number.isNaN`) or is not above zero, it changes nothing and returns
   `false`. Otherwise it adds the amount to the balance and returns `true`.
7. Add `withdraw(amount: number): boolean`. It returns `false` for the same two
   bad amounts and also when `amount` is larger than the balance. Otherwise it
   subtracts the amount and returns `true`.
8. Replace the object literal with `const account = new BankAccount('Alex', 100);`.
9. Change `showBalance` so the line reads `Alex: 120.00`, with the owner's name
   in front and the balance always carrying two decimal places. Research
   question 3 covers the second half.
10. Rewrite the Deposit listener. It hands `amountInput.valueAsNumber` to
    `account.deposit`. When the call returns `true` it clears `message`, and
    when it returns `false` it writes `Enter an amount above zero.` into
    `message`. Either way it calls `showBalance()`.
11. Rewrite the Withdraw listener the same way, with the message
    `Enter an amount above zero, and no more than your balance.`
12. Test it. Withdrawing 500 from 100 leaves the balance alone and shows the
    message in red. Clearing the number field and clicking Deposit does the
    same instead of turning the balance into `NaN`. Depositing 20 and
    withdrawing 20 gets you back to where you started.
13. Add `account.balanceValue = 1000000;` at the end of the file and run
    `npx tsc --noEmit`. Compare the error with what the object literal let you
    do in step 2, then delete the line.
